title: hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna
hook: a blue ring of flame on a gas stove. the Rig Veda's opening hymn asks that kind of fire to stay close

segments.voice: Yesterday closed a week on the Gayatri in context, ending with Krishna in the Gita: among meters, I am the Gayatri. Which side of that one verse stayed with you? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-eight.

Click, click, whoomp. A blue ring of flame on a gas stove. A match struck for a birthday candle. A lamp lit in a window. Fire is easy to use all day without a second thought. The Rig Veda opens with a hymn to that fire, and it doesn't treat it as a tool. It treats it as someone. For four days this path listens to four of the Veda's voices: Agni, Indra, Ushas and Varuna. Today: Agni, the fire.
screen: `CLICK, CLICK, WHOOMP.` → `NOT A TOOL. SOMEONE.` → `FOUR VOICES. TODAY, AGNI.`

segments.voice: Agni is the Sanskrit word for fire, and in the Vedas he is also the god in the fire. The hymn that opens the Rig Veda, book one, hymn one, begins agnim ile purohitam: I praise Agni, the one placed in front. He's called a priest, the one who calls the gods and carries the offering. When something is poured into the sacred fire, the hymn says, it's Agni who takes it to the gods. So fire stands in the middle: on the ground, in the house, and reaching up toward heaven. That's the familiar part. Two later verses of the same hymn bring it closer. One says, in paraphrase: to you, Agni, day after day, we come with our thoughts, bringing homage. Not on festival days only. Every day. Some translators also hear in that verse the edges of the day, dusk and dawn, the same hours the Gayatri is kept. And then the hymn's last verse, and it's a warm one. In Sanskrit, sa nah piteva sunave, agne supayano bhava. Be easy to approach for us, Agni, as a father is to his son. Stay with us, for our good. The great power that carries offerings to the gods is asked to be approachable. Not distant, not dangerous, not grand. Like a father a child can walk right up to. That's how the hymnbook begins: not with thunder, but with a fire in the house, asked to be near.
screen: `AGNI: FIRE, AND THE GOD IN IT.` · `THE PRIEST WHO CARRIES THE OFFERING.` · `DAY AFTER DAY, WITH HOMAGE.` · `EASY TO REACH, AS A FATHER TO A SON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch a small flame. If you have a candle or a lamp and it's safe, light it and set it a little way in front of you. If not, bring to mind a flame you know well: a stove, a diya, a birthday candle. Let your eyes rest on it. Notice how it never holds still, leaning, flickering, steadying again. Don't stare hard. Just keep it company. When your attention drifts, come back to the flame. If you pray, you can hold the hymn's last line in mind: be easy to approach, as a father to his son. The bell holds the time.
Hymns to Agni. Agni is fire, and the god in the fire, the priest who carries the offering, asked in the Rig Veda's opening hymn to be easy to approach, like a father to his son. Today's word.
Your line: hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna. Today, the next time you light a stove, a candle or a lamp, pause for one breath before you use it. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: In Vedic ritual, offerings are poured into a sacred fire while hymns to Agni are recited; at home, some Hindu households light a lamp at dawn or dusk, and some keep a fire offering, homa, on special days.
